\item[Continuous and continuously differentiable.]
$f\in C([0,1])$ means that $f$ is continuous on the closed interval.
$f\in C^1([0,1])$ means that both $f$ and its ordinary derivative $f'$ are
continuous.  The notation $C^2$ similarly asks for two continuous
derivatives.

\item[Weak derivative and $H^1$.]
A function can have a usable derivative even if it has corners.  A function
$g$ is the \emph{weak derivative} of $f$ when
\[
 \int_0^1 f(x)\varphi'(x)\dd x
 =-\int_0^1 g(x)\varphi(x)\dd x
\]
for every smooth test function $\varphi$ that vanishes near the endpoints.
The space $H^1(0,1)$ consists of functions for which both $f$ and this weak
derivative have finite squared integrals.  Ordinary differentiable functions
satisfy the same formula by integration by parts, so this is an extension of
the familiar derivative rather than a different operation.

\item[Test function.]
A test function is an arbitrary sufficiently regular function inserted into
an integral identity.  If two integrable expressions give the same integral
against every test function, they represent the same weak equation.

\item[Almost everywhere and almost surely.]
``Almost everywhere'' (a.e.) allows failure on a set of position-values of
length zero.  ``Almost surely'' (a.s.) allows failure on an event of
probability zero.  Neither phrase means ``approximately''; each is an exact
statement after ignoring a mathematically negligible set.

\item[Norm and supremum norm.]
A norm measures size.  For a vector $z=(z_1,\ldots,z_n)$,
$\|z\|_2=(\sum_jz_j^2)^{1/2}$.  For a bounded function,
\[
 \|f\|_\infty=\sup_{0\leq x\leq1}|f(x)|,
\]
the largest absolute height of its graph (or the least upper bound when the
largest value is approached but not reached).

\item[Hilbert space, linear functional, and coercivity.]
A Hilbert space is a vector space with a dot-product-like inner product in
which all Cauchy sequences have limits.  A linear functional turns a function
into a number while preserving addition and scalar multiplication.  It is
bounded if $|\Lambda(v)|\leq C\|v\|$ for one fixed $C$.  A bilinear form
$B(u,v)$ is linear in each input.  It is coercive if
$B(v,v)\geq c\|v\|^2$ for some $c>0$; informally, its energy cannot become
tiny while $v$ remains large.

\item[Eigenvector, eigenvalue, orthogonal basis, and Parseval.]
For a matrix $A$, a nonzero vector $v$ is an eigenvector with eigenvalue
$\lambda$ when $Av=\lambda v$.  Vectors are orthogonal when their dot product
is zero.  An orthogonal basis is a spanning set of mutually orthogonal
vectors.  Expanding $z=\sum_k c_ke_k$ in an orthonormal basis gives
Parseval's finite-dimensional identity $\|z\|_2^2=\sum_kc_k^2$, which is just
the Pythagorean theorem applied repeatedly.

\item[Compactness.]
In finite-dimensional Euclidean space, a set is compact exactly when it is
closed and bounded.  A continuous real-valued function on a nonempty compact
set attains both a minimum and a maximum.

\item[Big $O$ and little $o$.]
The statement $R(\varepsilon)=O(\varepsilon^2)$ means that constants $C$ and
$\varepsilon_0>0$ exist such that
$|R(\varepsilon)|\leq C\varepsilon^2$ whenever
$|\varepsilon|<\varepsilon_0$.  The statement
$R(\varepsilon)=o(\varepsilon)$ means
$R(\varepsilon)/\varepsilon\to0$.  These symbols describe a proved error
scale; they do not mean that the remainder is discarded.

\subsection{Elementary notation and calculus used throughout}

\subsubsection{Intervals, functions, and finite sums}

The closed interval
\[
 [0,1]=\{x\in\mathbb R:0\leq x\leq1\}
\]
is our physical corridor. The variable $x$ denotes position and $t\geq0$
denotes time. If $f$ is a function of position, then $f'(x)$ and $f''(x)$
denote its first and second derivatives wherever they exist.

The summation symbol means
\[
 \sum_{j=1}^{N}c_j=c_1+c_2+\cdots+c_N.
\]
Every such sum in this paper is finite. There is no convergence of an
infinite series hidden in our passage from point traps to integrals. When we
later write a finite sum as an integral against atoms, we use the exact
identity
\begin{equation}
 \int_0^1 \varphi(x)\,\mathrm d
 \left(\sum_{j=1}^{N}c_j\delta_{x_j}\right)
 =\sum_{j=1}^{N}c_j\varphi(x_j).
 \label{found:atomic-sum}
\end{equation}
Equation~\eqref{found:atomic-sum} is a change of notation, not a
series-to-integral approximation.

The indicator of a statement $A$ is
\[
 \mathbf 1_A=
 \begin{cases}
 1,&\text{if $A$ is true},\\
 0,&\text{if $A$ is false}.
 \end{cases}
\]
For example, $\mathbf 1_{\{x_j\leq x\}}$ jumps from $0$ to $1$ when $x$
passes $x_j$.

\subsection{Finite sums}

For numbers $z_1,\ldots,z_N$, the symbol
\[
\sum_{j=1}^{N}z_j=z_1+z_2+\cdots+z_N
\]
means ordinary finite addition.  Linearity says
\[
\sum_{j=1}^{N}(az_j+bw_j)
=a\sum_{j=1}^{N}z_j+b\sum_{j=1}^{N}w_j.
\]
Nothing in this formula involves a limit or an infinite series.

If $p_j>0$ and $\sum_jp_j=1$, then $(p_1,\ldots,p_N)$ is a probability
vector.  Its cumulative sums are
\[
q_0=0,
\qquad q_j=\sum_{i=1}^{j}p_i,
\qquad q_N=1.
\]
Subtracting consecutive cumulative sums recovers the original number:
\[
q_j-q_{j-1}
=\left(\sum_{i=1}^{j}p_i\right)
 -\left(\sum_{i=1}^{j-1}p_i\right)
=p_j.
\]

\subsection{The Fundamental Theorem of Calculus}

\begin{toolbox}{Fundamental Theorem of Calculus}
If $g$ is continuous and $G'(x)=g(x)$, then
\[
\int_a^b g(x)\dd x=G(b)-G(a).
\]
Equivalently, if $H(x)=\int_a^xg(s)\dd s$, then $H'(x)=g(x)$.
\end{toolbox}

Three antiderivatives used repeatedly are
\[
\int c\dd x=cx+C,
\qquad
\int x\dd x=\frac{x^2}{2}+C,
\qquad
\int x^2\dd x=\frac{x^3}{3}+C.
\]
For example,
\[
\int_{-h/2}^{h/2}s^2\dd s
=\left[\frac{s^3}{3}\right]_{-h/2}^{h/2}
=\frac{(h/2)^3-(-h/2)^3}{3}
=\frac{h^3}{12}.
\]
The constant $1/12$ in the stationary-average appendix theorem ultimately
comes from this exact one-cell integral.  The main worst-start theorem has
the different constant $1/8$ because it controls a maximum rather than an
integral average.

\subsection{Integration by parts}

\begin{toolbox}{integration by parts}
For differentiable $f,g$,
\[
\int_a^b f'(x)g(x)\dd x
=\bigl[f(x)g(x)\bigr]_{a}^{b}
-\int_a^b f(x)g'(x)\dd x.
\]
Equivalently,
\[
-\int_a^b f'(x)g(x)\dd x
=-\bigl[fg\bigr]_{a}^{b}+\int_a^b f(x)g'(x)\dd x.
\]
\end{toolbox}

This is the product rule integrated over an interval, because
$(fg)'=f'g+fg'$.

\begin{toolbox}{derivative of an inverse}
If $P$ is strictly increasing, differentiable, and $P'(x)>0$, then its inverse
$X=P^{-1}$ satisfies
\[
X'(y)=\frac1{P'(X(y))}.
\]
\end{toolbox}
Indeed, $P(X(y))=y$.  Differentiating both sides gives
$P'(X(y))X'(y)=1$, and division gives the displayed result.

\begin{toolbox}{change of variables in an integral}
For $y=P(x)$ with $P$ increasing,
\[
\int_{x=a}^{x=b}f(P(x))P'(x)\dd x
=\int_{y=P(a)}^{y=P(b)}f(y)\dd y.
\]
In differential shorthand, $\dd y=P'(x)\dd x$.
\end{toolbox}

\subsection{Cauchy--Schwarz and a two-vector consequence}

\begin{toolbox}{Cauchy--Schwarz inequality}
For real vectors $v,w$,
\[
\abs{v\mathbin\cdot w}\leq\norm v_2\norm w_2,
\qquad
\norm v_2^2=\sum_jv_j^2.
\]
\end{toolbox}

A form used in the stability proof is: for $A,B>0$,
\[
A\norm v_2^2+B\norm w_2^2
\geq\frac{AB}{A+B}\norm{v-w}_2^2.
\]
To verify it without guessing, multiply both sides by $A+B$ and subtract the
right-hand side:
\begin{align*}
&(A+B)(A\norm v^2+B\norm w^2)-AB\norm{v-w}^2\\
&=A^2\norm v^2+B^2\norm w^2+2AB(v\mathbin\cdot w)\\
&=\norm{Av+Bw}^2\geq0.
\end{align*}

\subsection{How a minimum is certified}

If an expression is written as
\[
Q=Q_{\min}+R_1+R_2+\cdots+R_m
\]
with every $R_i\geq0$, then $Q\geq Q_{\min}$.  Equality is possible only if
every $R_i=0$.  The main proof is built to obtain exactly this kind of
certificate; it does not merely differentiate and hope that a critical point
is global.

\subsubsection{The Dirac delta is an evaluation rule}

The Dirac delta at $x_j$, denoted $\delta_{x_j}$, is defined by
\begin{equation}
 \int_0^1\delta_{x_j}(x)v(x)\,\mathrm dx=v(x_j)
 \label{found:delta-definition}
\end{equation}
for every continuous test function $v$. It is not an ordinary function that
is infinite at one point and zero elsewhere. It is a distribution: a linear
rule acting on test functions.

Multiplying the delta by a number $c$ gives
\[
 \int_0^1c\delta_{x_j}(x)v(x)\,\mathrm dx=cv(x_j).
\]
Consequently,
\[
 \int_0^1\left(\sum_{j=1}^{N}c_j\delta_{x_j}(x)\right)v(x)\,\mathrm dx
 =\sum_{j=1}^{N}c_jv(x_j),
\]
which is the distributional version of \eqref{found:atomic-sum}.

\item[Martingale.]
A martingale $M_t$ is a fair-game process: conditional on everything observed
up to time $s<t$, its expected future value is the current value,
$\mathbb E[M_t\mid\mathcal F_s]=M_s$.  In particular, an integrable martingale
starting at zero has mean zero at every fixed time.

\item[Quadratic variation.]
For a rough path, quadratic variation is the limit of the sum of squared
increments,
\[
 \langle X\rangle_t
 =\lim_{\max|t_{i+1}-t_i|\to0}
   \sum_i\bigl(X_{t_{i+1}}-X_{t_i}\bigr)^2.
\]
For $X_t=\sqrt{2D}\,B_t$ it equals $2Dt$.  This identity explains the factor
$2D$ between two common normalizations of local time.

\paragraph{One-dimensional Sobolev continuity theorem (quoted).}
Every $H^1(0,1)$ function has a continuous representative, and evaluation
$u\mapsto u(x_j)$ is a continuous linear operation. Thus $u(x_j)$ in the
point-trap equation is meaningful; see, for example, the Sobolev-space
chapters of \cite{evans2010}.

For intuition, an $H^1$ function obeys the fundamental-theorem identity
\[
 u(x)=u(z)+\int_z^xu'(s)\,\mathrm ds.
\]
The Cauchy--Schwarz inequality gives
\begin{align*}
 |u(x)-u(z)|
 &\leq\int_z^x|u'(s)|\,\mathrm ds\\
 &\leq |x-z|^{1/2}
 \left(\int_0^1|u'(s)|^2\,\mathrm ds\right)^{1/2}.
\end{align*}
This estimate explains why a finite-energy one-dimensional function cannot
jump.

\paragraph{Local-time Feynman--Kac theorem (quoted).}
For reflected Brownian motion with generator $D\partial_{xx}$, occupation
local time normalized by \eqref{found:occupation-formula}, and positive point
reactivities $\kappa_j$, the function
\[
 u(x)=\mathbb E_x\left[\int_0^\infty
 e^{-\sum_j\kappa_j\ell_t^{x_j}}\,\mathrm dt\right]
\]
is the unique weak solution of
\begin{equation}
 \boxed{
 D\int_0^1u'(x)v'(x)\,\mathrm dx
 +\sum_{j=1}^{N}\kappa_ju(x_j)v(x_j)
 =\int_0^1v(x)\,\mathrm dx}
 \label{found:weak-constant}
\end{equation}
for every test function $v\in H^1(0,1)$.

This is the additive-functional form of Feynman--Kac; see
\cite{fitzsimmons1999}.  The normalization in
\eqref{found:occupation-formula} matters because it determines the
coefficient multiplying each point term.

The theorem can be proved using the It\^o--Tanaka formula applied to
$e^{-A_t}u(X_t)$, followed by stopping and limiting arguments. We quote that
stochastic theorem rather than reproduce its measure-theoretic proof. What we
do prove next is the exact relationship between the weak equation, its
piecewise classical form, and the flux identities used in the optimization.

\item[Hilbert space, linear functional, and coercivity.]
A Hilbert space is a vector space with a dot-product-like inner product in
which all Cauchy sequences have limits.  A linear functional turns a function
into a number while preserving addition and scalar multiplication.  It is
bounded if $|\Lambda(v)|\leq C\|v\|$ for one fixed $C$.  A bilinear form
$B(u,v)$ is linear in each input.  It is coercive if
$B(v,v)\geq c\|v\|^2$ for some $c>0$; informally, its energy cannot become
tiny while $v$ remains large.

\subsection{Why the weak problem has exactly one solution}

Define
\begin{align}
 B(u,v)
 &=D\int_0^1u'v'\,\mathrm dx
   +\sum_{j=1}^{N}\kappa_ju(x_j)v(x_j),
 \label{found:bilinear-form}\\
 \Lambda(v)&=\int_0^1v(x)\,\mathrm dx.
 \label{found:linear-form}
\end{align}
Then the weak problem is $B(u,v)=\Lambda(v)$ for every $v\in H^1(0,1)$.

\paragraph{Lax--Milgram theorem (quoted).}
Let $H$ be a Hilbert space. If $B:H\times H\to\mathbb R$ is a bounded
bilinear form, if $B(v,v)\geq c\|v\|_H^2$ for some $c>0$ and every $v$, and
if $\Lambda$ is a bounded linear functional, then there exists exactly one
$u\in H$ such that $B(u,v)=\Lambda(v)$ for every $v\in H$.
This standard existence theorem appears in functional-analysis treatments of
elliptic equations such as \cite{evans2010}.

Here $H=H^1(0,1)$. Boundedness follows from Cauchy--Schwarz and continuity of
point evaluation. Coercivity can be seen directly. Fix trap $x_1$. For every
$x$,
\[
 v(x)=v(x_1)+\int_{x_1}^{x}v'(s)\,\mathrm ds.
\]
Using $(a+b)^2\leq2a^2+2b^2$ and Cauchy--Schwarz,
\[
 |v(x)|^2\leq2|v(x_1)|^2+2\int_0^1|v'(s)|^2\,\mathrm ds.
\]
Integrating in $x$ gives
\begin{equation}
 \|v\|_{L^2}^2
 \leq2|v(x_1)|^2+2\|v'\|_{L^2}^2,
 \label{found:poincare-point}
\end{equation}
and consequently
\begin{equation}
 \|v\|_{H^1}^2
 \leq2|v(x_1)|^2+3\|v'\|_{L^2}^2.
 \label{found:H1-control}
\end{equation}
On the other hand,
\[
 B(v,v)
 \geq D\|v'\|_{L^2}^2+\kappa_1|v(x_1)|^2.
\]
Hence
\begin{equation}
 B(v,v)\geq
 \min\!\left\{\frac D3,\frac{\kappa_1}{2}\right\}
 \|v\|_{H^1}^2.
 \label{found:coercive}
\end{equation}
All Lax--Milgram hypotheses hold, so existence and uniqueness follow.

There is also an elementary uniqueness check. If $u_1$ and $u_2$ solve the
same weak equation, set $w=u_1-u_2$. Subtract their equations and choose
$v=w$:
\[
 D\int_0^1|w'|^2\,\mathrm dx
 +\sum_j\kappa_j|w(x_j)|^2=0.
\]
Every summand is nonnegative, so $w'=0$ and $w(x_j)=0$. Thus $w$ is a
constant that vanishes at a trap, and $w=0$.

\subsubsection{Why the lowest eigenvalue is positive}

Every term in the numerator of \eqref{eq:expanded-Rayleigh} is nonnegative,
so \(\lambda_1\ge0\).  If it were zero, a minimizing function \(v\ne0\)
would have to make every nonnegative term zero.  Thus
\[
  \int_0^L|v'|^2\dd y=0.
\]
The function \(|v'|^2\) need not be continuous for a general \(H^1\)
function, so we use the correct measure-theoretic statement: a nonnegative
integrable function with zero integral is zero almost everywhere.  Hence
\(v'=0\) almost everywhere.  The fundamental theorem for one-dimensional
Sobolev functions then says that \(v\) has a constant continuous
representative.  The trap terms would also have to vanish:
\[
  \kappa_j|v(x_j)|^2=0.
\]
Because \(\kappa_j>0\), this forces \(v(x_j)=0\), and a constant that is zero
at one point is zero everywhere.  That contradicts \(v\ne0\).  Therefore
\begin{equation}
  \lambda_1>0.
  \label{eq:expanded-positive-eigen}

source.exact_excerpt:
\subsubsection{Local time in the general reversible model}

For a nonuniform diffusion, several quantities in the literature are called
local time and differ by position-dependent factors. We remove the ambiguity
by specifying the additive functional through its Revuz measure.

\paragraph{Revuz correspondence (quoted theorem).}
For a symmetric Markov process with reference measure
$\pi(x)\,\mathrm dx$, positive continuous additive functionals correspond to
suitable positive measures called \emph{smooth measures}.  In the regular
one-dimensional reflected diffusion considered here, interior points are
nonpolar, so each unit atom $\delta_{x_j}$ is an admissible smooth measure.
The point local time used here is the additive functional whose Revuz measure
is that atom.  See \cite{fukushima2011} for the general correspondence.

An elementary reader may treat this as a normalization rule: it is the
local-time convention for which a trap of strength $\kappa_j$ appears in the
weak equation as
\[
 \kappa_ju(x_j)v(x_j).
\]
No later algebra requires the abstract construction of Revuz measures. What
matters is that one convention is used consistently in the probability model
and the weak equation.

\subsection{A dictionary between physical and transformed variables}

\[
\begin{array}{c|c|c}
\text{quantity}&\text{physical coordinate }x&\text{stationary coordinate }y\\
\hline
\text{coordinate}&x&y=P(x)\\
\text{inverse coordinate}&x&x=X(y)=P^{-1}(y)\\
\text{mean lifetime}&u(x)&U(y)=u(X(y))\\
\text{trap position}&x_j&y_j=P(x_j)\\
\text{source density}&\pi(x)&1\\
\text{conductance}&a(x)&b(y)=a(X(y))\pi(X(y))\\
\text{metric weight}&\text{not isolated}&\omega(y)=1/b(y)\\
\text{diffusive flux}&a(x)u'(x)&b(y)U'(y)\\
\text{absorbed flux}&\kappa_ju(x_j)&p_j=\kappa_jU(y_j).
\end{array}
\]

As a consistency check, set $\pi\equiv1$ and $a\equiv D$. Then
\[
 P(x)=x,\qquad X(y)=y,\qquad b(y)=D,\qquad\omega(y)=\frac1D.
\]
The generalized flux law becomes $DU'(y)=F(y)-y$, and the energy identity
becomes
\[
 \overline u
 =\sum_j\frac{p_j^2}{\kappa_j}
 +\frac1D\int_0^1(F(y)-y)^2\,\mathrm dy,
\]
which is precisely \eqref{found:constant-energy} after renaming $y$ as $x$.

source.exact_excerpt:
Standard one-dimensional maximum-principle theory says that the minimizing
eigenfunction can be chosen strictly positive and that it is unique up to a
constant multiplier.  This is the only standard spectral fact we quote
without rebuilding functional analysis from its axioms.  Positivity will be
crucial: it prevents the angle introduced below from making a hidden jump by
\(\pi\).

We quoted the standard existence, positivity, and simplicity theorem for the
ground state of a one-dimensional Schr\"odinger operator with positive point
interactions, and the standard spectral expansion giving the long-time
survival asymptotic.  Those facts belong to established operator theory.

\begin{toolbox}{one-dimensional ground-state theorem}
For a regular one-dimensional self-adjoint Sturm--Liouville problem with
separated endpoint conditions and finitely many real delta interactions, the
lowest eigenvalue is simple and has an eigenfunction that is strictly
positive on the open interval.  Every higher eigenfunction has a zero.
This is the one-dimensional Sturm oscillation theorem.
\end{toolbox}

source.exact_excerpt:
\subsubsection{The differential and jump equations}

Because of \eqref{eq:expanded-positive-eigen}, write
\begin{equation}
 \lambda_1=Dk^2,
 \qquad k=\sqrt{\lambda_1/D}>0.
 \label{eq:expanded-k-definition}
\end{equation}
Let \(\phi>0\) denote its eigenfunction.  Away from a trap the Dirac terms
vanish, so
\[
 -D\phi''=\lambda_1\phi=Dk^2\phi.
\]
Divide by the positive number \(D\) and move the right side to the left:
\begin{equation}
  \phi''+k^2\phi=0.
  \label{eq:expanded-free-ode}
\end{equation}
The reflecting endpoint conditions are
\begin{equation}
  \phi'(0)=0,
  \qquad
  \phi'(L)=0.
  \label{eq:expanded-Neumann}
\end{equation}

To find the derivative jump at \(x_j\), integrate the formal eigenvalue
equation from \(x_j-\eta\) to \(x_j+\eta\):
\[
 -D\int_{x_j-\eta}^{x_j+\eta}\phi''(y)\dd y
 +\kappa_j\int_{x_j-\eta}^{x_j+\eta}
       \delta_{x_j}(y)\phi(y)\dd y
 =\lambda_1\int_{x_j-\eta}^{x_j+\eta}\phi(y)\dd y.
\]
The fundamental theorem of calculus makes the first integral
\[
 -D\bigl(\phi'(x_j+\eta)-\phi'(x_j-\eta)\bigr).
\]
The Dirac evaluation rule makes the second integral \(\kappa_j\phi(x_j)\).
The ordinary integral on the right tends to zero as \(\eta\downarrow0\).
Taking that limit gives
\[
 -D\bigl(\phi'(x_j+)-\phi'(x_j-)\bigr)
 +\kappa_j\phi(x_j)=0,
\]
or, equivalently,
\begin{equation}
 D\bigl(\phi'(x_j+)-\phi'(x_j-)\bigr)
 =\kappa_j\phi(x_j).
 \label{eq:expanded-jump}
\end{equation}
The function itself stays continuous; only its slope jumps upward.

source.exact_excerpt:
\begin{toolbox}{Jensen's inequality for a concave function}
If \(g\) is concave and \(t_1,\ldots,t_N\) lie in its interval, then
\[
 \frac1N\sum_{j=1}^Ng(t_j)
 \le g\left(\frac1N\sum_{j=1}^Nt_j\right).
\]
If \(g\) is strictly concave, equality is possible only when all
\(t_j\) are equal.
\end{toolbox}

For fixed \(k>0\), define
\[
 g(t)=\arctan\left(\frac{t}{2Dk}\right),
 \qquad t>0.
\]
To check strict concavity rather than merely assert it, put \(c=2Dk>0\).
Then
\[
 g'(t)=\frac{1/c}{1+(t/c)^2}=\frac{c}{c^2+t^2},
\]
and differentiation once more gives
\begin{equation}
 g''(t)=-\frac{2ct}{(c^2+t^2)^2}<0.
 \label{eq:expanded-arctan-concavity}
\end{equation}
Therefore Jensen and \eqref{eq:expanded-budget} imply
\[
 \frac1N\sum_jg(\kappa_j)
 \le g\left(\frac1N\sum_j\kappa_j\right)
 =g(K/N).
\]

\begin{toolbox}{changing the order on a triangle}
If $g$ is continuous, then
\[
 \int_0^\alpha\int_q^\alpha g(s)\dd s\dd q
 =\int_0^\alpha\int_0^s g(s)\dd q\dd s
 =\int_0^\alpha s g(s)\dd s.
\]
The first integral covers the triangle $0\leq q\leq s\leq\alpha$.
Similarly,
\[
 \int_\alpha^1\int_\alpha^q g(s)\dd s\dd q
 =\int_\alpha^1(1-s)g(s)\dd s.
\]
This finite-rectangle result is the elementary continuous form of Fubini's
theorem.
\end{toolbox}

source.exact_excerpt:
\subsubsection{Neumann and Dirichlet limits}

If $\beta=0$, then
\[
 B(k)=\arctan0=0,
\]
and the Robin condition becomes $\phi'=0$, which is the Neumann condition.
Thus Neumann endpoints are included exactly, not merely as a limit.

If $\beta\to\infty$, then
\[
 B(k)=\arctan\frac{\beta}{Dk}\longrightarrow\frac\pi2.
\]
A finite-energy Robin eigenfunction is forced toward zero at that endpoint,
which is the Dirichlet condition.  The phase $\pm\pi/2$ is also exactly the
phase of a zero of $\phi$, because $\cos(\pm\pi/2)=0$ in
\eqref{eq:exp-x16-phase-vector}.

We also verify that the optimized roots and sites really converge, rather
than only the displayed angle at a fixed $k$.  Let one or both positive
endpoint coefficients increase to infinity while all interior data stay
fixed.  Increasing an endpoint coefficient increases its $B$ term at every
fixed $k$, so the unique crossing in \eqref{eq:exp-x16-root} moves to the
right.  The roots are bounded above by the unique solution of the limiting
equation obtained by replacing each diverging $B$ term by $\pi/2$.  Hence the
increasing roots have a finite limit $\bar k>0$.  Along the roots,
\[
 \arctan\frac{\beta}{Dk_\beta}\longrightarrow\frac\pi2,
\]
because $k_\beta$ stays bounded.  Passing to the limit in the root equation
shows that $\bar k$ solves the limiting Dirichlet phase equation.  That
equation has only one positive root, so $\bar k$ is the Dirichlet root.
Finally, every term in the site formula \eqref{eq:exp-x16-sites} is
continuous in the root and the endpoint phases, so all maximizing sites
converge to the corresponding Dirichlet-site formula as well.

As a basic check with no interior interactions, one Neumann and one
Dirichlet endpoint give
\[
 kL=0+\frac\pi2,
 \qquad k=\frac\pi{2L},
\]
and two Dirichlet endpoints give $kL=\pi$.  These are the familiar first
wavenumbers of the mixed and Dirichlet interval problems.  The theorem itself
assumes positive interior interactions; the no-interaction calculation is a
boundary-limit consistency check.

Merely each state having finite energy, without normalization/uniform bound, does not force its endpoint values to zero; the source shorthand must be read with these explicit conditions. No entire operator/state convergence is being asserted.

claims.claim: Finite nondifferentiable Karamata, strict permutation equality, and finite balancing/permutation characterization.

source.exact_excerpt:
\begin{toolbox}{finite Karamata inequality}
Let $x,y\in I^N$ have the same sum.  If $x\succeq y$ and $f$ is concave on
the interval $I$, then
\[
 \sum_{j=1}^Nf(x_j)\leq\sum_{j=1}^Nf(y_j).
\]
If $f$ is strictly concave and $x$ is not a permutation of $y$, the
inequality is strict.
\end{toolbox}

Here is why the direction points that way.  Suppose $a>b$ and transfer a
small amount $\varepsilon$ from $a$ to $b$, with
$0<\varepsilon\leq(a-b)/2$.  Define
\[
 H(\varepsilon)=f(a-\varepsilon)+f(b+\varepsilon).
\]
Then
\[
 H'(\varepsilon)
 =-f'(a-\varepsilon)+f'(b+\varepsilon).
\]
For a concave differentiable function, $f'$ is decreasing.  Since
$b+\varepsilon\leq a-\varepsilon$, we have
$f'(b+\varepsilon)\geq f'(a-\varepsilon)$ and hence
$H'(\varepsilon)\geq0$.  Balancing a pair cannot decrease the sum of a
concave function; strict concavity makes the increase strict unless no
balancing occurs.

The finite Hardy--Littlewood--P\'olya characterization of majorization says
that $y$ can be reached from $x\succeq y$ by finitely many such balancing
transfers and a permutation.  Repeating the two-number calculation proves
Karamata's inequality in the form used here.  Thus no unexplained
``black-box direction'' remains.
